title: Does Qwen 3.5 9B know a test when nobody says so?
question: The same transfer test on the 9B instruct model: trained on explicit cues, scored on implicit ones, against the words alone and a formality probe.

summary.headline: best layer 7: 100% on new wording (words alone 55%, word meanings 87%, formality 70%, shuffled labels at most 70%)

claims.text: It carries over to new wording: trained on the 120 texts of eval_deploy and scored on 60 texts of eval_deploy_implicit (other items, other cues), a logistic probe at layer 7 gets 100% right (exact 95% interval 94.0% to 100.0%), against 70% at best for probes trained and scored on shuffled labels. Its cut is re-centred, and the layer picked, on 60 other texts of the new set.
claims.test: CI lower bound clears the best shuffled-label probe by 5 points

claims.text: It carries over by layer 1 of 32: earlier layers do not clear the control.
claims.test: first layer whose CI lower bound clears the control

claims.text: It is more than shared words: a probe on which tokens each text contains, with no model at all, trained on the same texts and re-centred the same way, gets 55% of the same held-out examples right (41.6% to 67.9%), against 100% at layer 7 (exact McNemar test on the 27 examples where they disagree: p = 1.5e-08).
claims.test: the best layer beats the words-only probe on the same held-out examples, exact McNemar p below 0.05

claims.text: It is more than word meanings: a probe on each text's average input embedding (what its words mean to the model before any layer combines them), trained on the same texts and re-centred the same way, gets 87% of the same held-out examples right (75.4% to 94.1%), against 100% at layer 7 (exact McNemar test on the 8 examples where they disagree: p = 0.0078).
claims.test: the best layer beats the word-meaning probe on the same held-out examples, exact McNemar p below 0.05

claims.text: It is not just formality: a probe trained to read formality on its own set (formal_casual), pointed the way formality runs in the training texts and re-centred like the probe, gets 70% of the same held-out examples right (56.8% to 81.2%), against 100% at layer 7 (exact McNemar test on the 18 examples where they disagree: p = 7.6e-06).
claims.test: the best layer beats the rival-property probe on the same held-out examples, exact McNemar p below 0.05

claims.text: It is more than any direction: 32 random directions at layer 7, each pointed the way it splits the training texts and re-centred like the probe, get 52% of the same held-out examples right on average and 83% at best, against 100% (exact 95% interval 94.0% to 100.0%).
claims.test: CI lower bound clears the best random direction by 5 points

claims.text: The simple difference-of-means direction at layer 7 gets 93% (83.8% to 98.2%); it is saved for steering, which tests whether the model actually uses it.

notes: The probe trains on all 120 texts of eval_deploy. The 120 texts of eval_deploy_implicit are new to it: 60 re-centre each probe's cut and pick the layer, and the other 60 are scored, whole pairs on each side. Every control is trained and scored the same way on the same texts.
What the words mean carries the label: a probe on each text's average input embedding gets 87% of the new texts with no context and no word order, so what the layers add is the step from 87% to 100%.

Random directions separate these texts too: at layer 7 the best of 32 gets 83% (average 52%). The two kinds of text differ in so many ways there that a direction picked at random reads the label, so the probe's direction is only as special as its lead over them.
